```{r setup, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library("DT") # Interactive HTML tables
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
```

Here we describe the the data and the results of the regional (2nd order) assessment of reindeer selection for grazing sites in the Malå reindeer herding community, Sweden, under the presence of mining and wind power development, for the three snow-free seasons: calving, summer, and autumn. We describe:

- the reindeer GPS data used for the analyses;
- how the analysis was set up: 
- the results of the habitat selection analysis (HSA).

# Goals of the analysis

The main question driving the HSA analyses is: how is the selection of grazing sites by reindeer across seasons affected by wind power, mining, and other human infrastructure and activity, at a large (regional) scale? In other words, how does reindeer selects for habitat at a 2nd order selection [sensu @johnson_comparison_1980]?

Specific questions:

-   Are there cumulative impacts of multiple disturbance of the same type, e.g. multiple turbines or multiple wind parks?
-   Are there cumulative impacts of different types of disturbance, e.g. both wind power and mining?
-   What is the zone of influence of the impacts, i.e. up to which distance from disturbance is reindeer behavior altered?
-   How does the impacts change across seasons - calving, summer, and autumn?

# Methods

## Data

```{r load_data, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
load("../../data/01_GPS/05_annotated_data/data_annotated_calving_ready_2h_rsf.RData")
load("../../data/01_GPS/05_annotated_data/data_annotated_summer_ready_2h_rsf.RData")
load("../../data/01_GPS/05_annotated_data/data_annotated_autumn_ready_2h_rsf.RData")

# calving
summ_calving_year <- data_ready_calving_rsf_2h |> 
  dplyr::filter(case_ == TRUE) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(year) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(n = n(),
                   n_ind = length(unique(id)))

summ_calving <- apply(summ_calving_year, 2, sum)

# summer
summ_summer_year <- data_ready_summer_rsf_2h |> 
  dplyr::filter(case_ == TRUE) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(year) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(n = n(),
                   n_ind = length(unique(id)))

summ_summer <- apply(summ_summer_year, 2, sum)

# autumn
summ_autumn_year <- data_ready_autumn_rsf_2h |> 
  dplyr::group_by(year) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(n = n(),
                   n_ind = length(unique(id)))

summ_autumn <- apply(summ_autumn_year, 2, sum)
```

The analysis was based on data of `{r} summ_calving[3]` reindeer tracked during calving, `{r} summ_summer[3]` during summer, and `{r} summ_autumn[3]` during autumn, collected between 2008 and 2018. Table C2 shows the number of individuals and number of used GPS positions recorded in each year.

```{r data_summary_year, echo=FALSE}
#| label: data_summary_year
#| fig-cap: "Table C2. Number of reindeer monitored (number of GPS positions recorded) in each year and season."
#| 
summ_data <- summ_calving_year |>
  dplyr::mutate(Phase = c(rep("Before construction", 2),
                          rep("Construction", 2),
                          rep("Operation", 4)),
                .after = 1) |> 
  dplyr::rename(`n - calving` = n,
                `number individuals - calving` = n_ind) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(
    summ_summer_year |> 
      dplyr::rename(`n - summer` = n,
                `number individuals - summer` = n_ind),
    by = "year"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(
    summ_autumn_year |> 
      dplyr::rename(`n - autumn` = n,
                `number individuals - autumn` = n_ind),
    by = "year"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::rename(Year = year) |> 
  dplyr::relocate(starts_with("number"), .after = "Phase")

summ_data |> 
  dplyr::mutate(Calving = paste0(`number individuals - calving`, " (", `n - calving`, ")"),
                Summer = paste0(`number individuals - summer`, " (", `n - summer`, ")"),
                Autumn = paste0(`number individuals - autumn`, " (", `n - autumn`, ")")) |> 
  dplyr::select(Year, Phase, Calving, Summer, Autumn) |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

## Statistical modeling

We modeled habitat selection using binomial regression following [@fieberg_how_2021]. Used GPS positions were compared to available positions spread randomly throughout the availability area within each season. The area available was different across seasons (see Figs AXXX in Appendix A) and it was defined by the reindeer herding community borders on the North, West, and South, and the fence **HOW TO CALL THIS FENCE?** in the East during calving. In summer and autumn the animals often cross the fence, so the eastern limits of the availability area were defined by a buffer around the used positions, accounting for the reindeer herding community borders and the main roads. 

We ran models using use/availability as a response variable and the effects of wind power, mining, and other infrastructure (private and public roads, power lines, houses, trails) as covariates. We also added other land cover and phenology related variables - elevation, slope, aspect, terrain position index, and dat of the start of the season (SOS) (or end of season, EOS, for autumn). SOS and EOS are phenological variables based on NDVI that show the peak greening and browning of the vegetation in spring and autumn. Given our questions, our focus was mainly on estimating the impacts of wind power and mining, so the other variables were mainly included to control for their possible, additive effects.

We assessed if and how the impacts of wind power and mining accumulated using the approach from Niebuhr et al. [-@niebuhr_estimating_2023]. To represent the spatial influence of wind power and mining, we computed zones of influence (ZOI) that decayed exponentially from the disturbance source and vanished at varying distances, from 100 m to 10 km. For wind power, we computed both the cumulative ZOI and the ZOI of the nearest feature; for mining we only considered the ZOI of the nearest mine, since there is only one main mining site in the study area. For simplicity, the influence of all other infrastructure types was modeled using the log-distance to the nearest feature. We built binomial regression models using each possible combination of ZOI radii and type (cumulative vs. nearest) for wind power and different ZOI radii for mining, together with different scales for the TPI and an additive effect of all the other variables. To evaluate the impact of wind turbines, we used a before-after set up, comparing the selection for the ZOI of wind turbines across construction phases - before construction, during construction, and operation.

The overall model structure we fitted was the following:

```{r}
base_formula <- case_ ~ 
  scale(dem) + I(scale(dem)^2) + scale(slope) + cos_aspect + 
  scale(sos) + 
  log(power_lines_dist+1) + log(priv_road_dist+1) + log(public_road_dist+1) + 
  log(trails_dist+1) + 
  log(house_dist+1) + scale(mining_Krist_nearestXXX) +
  wf_name + landcover*phase*scale(wind_turbines_ZZZ)
  # + tpi_scale_TTT
```

where `case_` is our response variable, `dem` is elevation, `phase` is the construction phase, and `wf_name` is the name of the wind farm closest to each point, to account for different behaviors around each of them. The model includes the logarithm of the distance to the nearest infrastructure for power lines, roads, trails, and houses, the ZOI of the mine, and an interaction beween land cover, phase, and the ZOI of wind turbines.

To evaluate the most likely ZOI for the mine and the wind turbines, whether there was a cumulative impact of multiple wind farms, and at which scale the TPI most affected reindeer movement, we replaced these variables in the model structure above using each possible combination of ZOI radii and type (cumulative vs. nearest) for wind power and the different ZOI radii for mining, together with different scales for the TPI. Models were compared through the Akaike information criterion (AIC), and the most parsimonious model was selected as the one with smaller AIC [@burnham_model_2002].

To interpret the results, we first checked the structure of the best ranking models (through the AIC and their difference; we considered model evidence different if dAIC > 2; Burnham and Anderson 2002) and compared how they differed qualitatively. Second, we evaluated the coefficients of the best random model for each season. We plotted the relative selection strength [RSS; @avgar_relative_2017] for wind turbines and land cover, as well as for mining, using the function [ggpredict()] from the package `ggeffects`.

# Results

## Model selection

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# calving
load("../../output/rsf_calving_multi_zoi_table_landcover_grouped.rda")
tab_models_calving <- tab_models[-1]
form_calving <- tab_models_calving$definition[1] |> 
  gsub(pattern = "\n   ", replacement = "")
# summer
load("../../output/rsf_summer_multi_zoi_table_landcover_grouped.rda")
tab_models_summer <- tab_models
form_summer <- tab_models_summer$definition[1] |> 
  gsub(pattern = "\n   ", replacement = "")
# autumn
load("../../output/rsf_autumn_multi_zoi_table_landcover.rda")
tab_models_autumn <- tab_models
form_autumn <- tab_models_autumn$definition[1] |> 
  gsub(pattern = "\n   ", replacement = "")
```

Summary of best ranked models:

-   Calving: Log-distance to the nearest feature, viewshed\
    `y ~ wind_zoi_nearest_5km*phase*landcover + mining_zoi_nearest_10km + ...`

-   Summer: Log-distance to the nearest feature, viewshed\
    `y ~ wind_zoi_cumulative_10km*phase*viewshed + mining_zoi_nearest_10km + ...`

-   Autumn: ZoI of the nearest feature with radius = 10km, land cover\
    `y ~ wind_zoi_nearest_10km*phase*landcover + mining_zoi_nearest_10km + ...`

### Calving

Table B3 shows the ranking of most parsimonious model for 2nd order habitat selection 
during calving. The best model for calving included the additive effect of mining at 10 km radius and 
of the zone of influence of the nearest wind turbine at 5 km radius (Table B3). 
The second, third, and forth ranking models also included ZOI of the nearest wind turbine
at large scales, which does not support the hypothesis of cumulative impacts of multiple 
wind turbines or parks during calving. All the best ranking models support a large ZOI radius
for both the mine (10 km) and the wind turbines (5-10 km).

```{r aic_calving, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
#| label: aic_calving
#| fig-cap: "Table B2. Table of model selection for the HSA models for calving. Columns are zone of influence (ZOI) radius for mining and wind turbines, scale for the terrain position index (TPI), AIC of the model, dAIC of each model in relation to the most parsimonious model, and the formula with each model's structure. Variables with 'Log' correspond to the log-distance to the nearest feature for that variable."

aic_calving <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_AIC_table_complete.csv")

aic_calving |> 
  dplyr::mutate(dAIC = round(dAIC - dAIC[1], digits = 2),
                aic = round(aic, digits = 2),
                tpi = sub("tpi_cat_s", "", tpi)) |> 
  dplyr::relocate(definition, .after = last_col()) |> 
  dplyr::select(-lc) |>
  dplyr::rename(`Mining ZOI radius` = 1,
                `Wind turbine ZOI radius` = 2,
                TPI = tpi,
                AIC = aic,
                formula = definition) |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

### Summer

Table B4 shows the ranking of most parsimonious model for 2nd order habitat selection 
during summer. The best model for summer included the additive effect of mining at 10km radius and 
of the cumulative zone of influence (density) of wind turbines at 10 km radius (Table B4).
However, the effect size of the wind turbines was small (see Table B8 and Fig B2 below).
All the best ranking models support a large ZOI radius for both the mine (5 - 10 km) and 
the wind turbines (5-10 km).

### Autumn

Table B5 shows the ranking of most parsimonious model for 2nd order habitat selection 
during autumn. The best model for autumn included the additive effect of mining at 10km radius and 
of the zone of influence of the nearest wind turbine at 10km radius (Table B5).

the wind turbines (5-10 km).

## Disturbance effects

### Coefficients - general

Here we show the coefficient estimates for all the infrastructure types, excluding wind turbines which present interactions in the model
structure and are explored further down. The estimates are put together for the different seasons in table B6 
so it is easy to compare the effects between them.

The mine was strongly avoided in all seasons, mainly during calving. Public roads was also
avoided in all seasons. Trails and private/dirt roads were avoided during calving and 
summer, but were selected in autumn (**why??**). Power lines were avoided only during calving 
and were selected in the other seasons. Houses were avoided during autumn, but were 
select during calving and summer (*why??*)

Discuss here:

- effect of houses
- effects during autumn
- should we add the land cover types here?

```{r coef_general, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
#| label: coef_general
#| fig-cap: "Table B6. Coefficient estimates for the infrastructure types and the start/end of season for all three seasons."
#| 
# read calving
coef_calving <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_coef_table_.csv") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(significant = as.factor(if_else(p.value < 0.05, 1, 0)),
                p = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", round(p.value, 3)),
                select = case_when(
                  (estimate > 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate < 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "avoidance",
                  (estimate < 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate > 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "selection",
                  TRUE ~ "no effect"
                ))

# read summer
coef_summer <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_summer_coef_table_log.csv") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(significant = as.factor(if_else(p.value < 0.05, 1, 0)),
                p = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", round(p.value, 3)),
                select = case_when(
                  (estimate > 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate < 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "avoidance",
                  (estimate < 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate > 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "selection",
                  TRUE ~ "no effect"
                ))

# read autumn
coef_autumn <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_coef_table_zoi.csv") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(significant = as.factor(if_else(p.value < 0.05, 1, 0)),
                p = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", round(p.value, 3)),
                select = case_when(
                  (estimate > 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate < 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "avoidance",
                  (estimate < 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate > 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "selection",
                  TRUE ~ "no effect"
                ))

coef_all <- dplyr::tibble(season = c(rep("calving", nrow(coef_calving)), 
                          rep("summer", nrow(coef_summer)),
                          rep("autumn", nrow(coef_autumn)))) |> 
  cbind(
    dplyr::bind_rows(coef_calving, coef_summer, coef_autumn)) |> 
  dplyr::filter(grepl("log|nearest|sos|eos", term)) |> 
  dplyr::filter(!grepl("wind", term)) |> 
  dplyr::select(-c(statistic, significant, p.value)) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(term)

coef_all |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

## Model predictions

Here we plot, for each season, the effect of the mine and the wind turbines, while
keeping all the other variables at their median values, to illustrate the mean
effect of these two types of infrastructure.

### Calving

Effect of the mine:

![Figure B1. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the mine in Kristineberget in calving.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_mining.png)

Effect of the wind turbines before, during, and after the construction of the wind farms, for different land use types:

![Figure B2. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the nearest wind turbine in calving, using Jokkmokksliden wind park as a reference.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_wind_phase_landcc_jokkmokksliden.png)

Open lands, clear cuts, coniferous forests, and mires were avoided up to 2.5-5 km from the
wind turbines, when we compare the reindeer behavior before and during (after) the 
construction of the turbines. Deciduous forests and forested wetlands in the proximity 
of the wind parks were also avoided during construction phase, but deciduous forests
were slightly more strongly selected in the operation phase, if compared to the baseline.


The effect is qualitatively similar for all when reindeer are closer to each of the four wind parks, but is smaller when
close to Åmliden wind park in the Southeast, most probably because of joint effect of the fence which is a barrier for
reindeer movement.

**Do we need to add the other figures for each wind park?**

### Summer

Effect of the mine:

![Figure B3. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the mine in Kristineberget in summer.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_summer_mining.png)

Effect of the wind turbines before, during, and after the construction of the wind farms, for different land use types:

![Figure B4. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the nearest wind turbine in summer, using Jokkmokksliden wind park as a reference.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_summer_wind_phase_landcc_jokkmokksliden.png)

### Autumn

Effect of the mine:

![Figure B5. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the mine in Kristineberget in autumn.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_mining.png)

Effect of the wind turbines before, during, and after the construction of the wind farms, for different land use types:

![Figure B6. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the nearest wind turbine in autumn, using Storliden wind park as a reference.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_wind_phase_landcc_storliden.png)

In the proximity of the wind turbines, deciduous forests, forested wetlands, and mires 
were avoided more strongly in the construction and operation phases, compared to the 
baseline. Urban areas were also more avoided in the operation phase. In contrast,
open areas were used more often in the construction phase than in the baseline
(**does it make sense??**)

The effect is qualitatively similar for all when reindeer are closer to each of the four wind parks, but is smaller when
close to Åmliden wind park in the Southeast, most probably because of joint effect of the fence which is a barrier for
reindeer movement.

## Spatial predictions

Here we show the baseline habitat suitability for each season before the construction of the wind turbines.
We also show the difference in habitat suitability between for the wind turbine construction and operation
phases, in comparison with the baseline habitat suitability.

#### Calving

![Figure B7.](../../output/rsf_results/maps_calving.png)


#### Summer

![Figure B8.](../../output/rsf_results/maps_summer.png)

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# read prediction rasters
dir <- "../../output/spatial_predictions/"
summer_files <- list.files(dir, full.names = T, pattern = "summer")
summer_maps <- terra::rast(summer_files)
# plot(calving_maps)

# read wind turbines vector
dir2 <- "../../maps/shp/"
wt_file <- list.files(dir2, full.names = T, pattern = "wind") |> 
  grep(pattern = ".shp$", value = T)
wt <- sf::st_read(wt_file)

# read mine vector
mine_file <- list.files(dir2, full.names = T, pattern = "mine") |> 
  grep(pattern = ".shp$", value = T)
mine <- sf::st_read(mine_file)

# plot
summer_maps <- summer_maps * 1
tm_shape(summer_maps) +
  tm_raster(palette = "Greens") +
  tm_shape(wt, is.master = T) +
  tm_dots() +
  tm_shape(mine) +
  tm_borders(col = "red")

# normalize 97.5%
summer_max <- terra::global(summer_maps[[1]], quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = T)[1,1]
summer_maps <- terra::ifel(summer_maps > summer_max, summer_max, summer_maps)
summer_maps <- oneimpact::raster_rescale(summer_maps)                         
# plot(summer_maps)

tm_shape(summer_maps) +
  tm_raster(palette = "Greens") +
  tm_shape(wt, is.master = T) +
  tm_dots() +
  tm_shape(mine) +
  tm_borders(col = "red")

summer_BA <- summer_maps[[3]] - summer_maps[[1]]
summer_BD <- summer_maps[[2]] - summer_maps[[1]]
summer_comparison <- c(summer_BD, summer_BA)
names(summer_comparison) <- c("before-during", "before-after")
# plot(calving_comparison)
tm_shape(summer_comparison) +
  tm_raster(palette = "PRGn") +
  tm_shape(wt, is.master = T) +
  tm_dots() +
  tm_shape(mine) +
  tm_borders(col = "red")
#tmaptools::palette_explorer()
```
